Good weekend, everyone. Before we begin today’s lecture, I’d like to express my sincere gratitude to all the industry colleagues who have been following my videos and supporting my channel. In the future, I will continue to produce more high-quality, valuable video content to share with you all.

Today, I’d like to share with you two essential reference books for electrical engineering professionals, which are regarded as technical authorities, encyclopedias, and even industry bibles. These two sets are the IEEE Color Books and the BICSI Guides.

The IEEE Color Books and the BICSI Guides are essential reference resources for electrical engineering professionals, widely regarded as technical authorities, encyclopedic references, and industry standards.  

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) is a leading global organization in electrical and electronics engineering. It develops and maintains numerous international standards, publishes extensive technical literature, and supports a broad range of technical committees spanning diverse engineering disciplines. IEEE also organizes major annual academic conferences, making it a central hub for innovation and scholarly exchange in the field.

IEEE membership is divided into several tiers: regular member, Senior Member, Fellow, and Life Fellow. I recall that back in the 1980s when I was studying at Tsinghua University, most domestic professors had not yet joined IEEE. About a decade ago, I applied for IEEE membership—the process was relatively straightforward: submit an application, pay the membership fee, and provide a resume. To become a Senior Member, however, requires recommendation letters from two existing Senior Members. As for Fellow or Life Fellow status, applicants must demonstrate outstanding academic achievements and publish extensively.

Although IEEE membership requires annual fees (I’ve paused my renewal in recent years), joining remains a wise choice for professionals seeking academic advancement in the power electronics field. Notably, IEEE includes the Standards Association (IEEE SA), which is responsible for developing various industry standards.

Next, we will introduce IEEE’s Color Books. This set of technical literature consists of 13 volumes, named for their distinct cover colors. It provides comprehensive guidance covering design, construction, and maintenance, with the entire collection totaling approximately 6,000 pages.

You can purchase them through the IEEE official website or other distribution channels (such as Amazon), available in both hardcover and paperback editions. IEEE members are eligible for a discount of approximately 10%.

As an essential reference for power system engineers, IEEE Color Books have proven to be one of the most valuable resources throughout my 30-year career. I purchased this set in 2009 for nearly 2,000 Canadian dollars and still consider it a worthwhile investment to this day.

Below is a list of IEEE Color Books, each corresponding to an IEEE standard. For instance, the first one, IEEE Standard 141, also known as the Red Book, primarily addresses industrial power distribution systems, covering topics such as grounding systems. There are a total of 13 such standards.

Since June 20, 2012, IEEE has published a set of standards called the IEEE 3000 Standards Collection to replace the original IEEE Color Books. These standards are specifically designed for industrial and commercial power systems. The provided link directs to the relevant page on IEEE’s official website.

As you can see, this provides a detailed introduction to the IEEE 3000 standard set.

First, the IEEE 3001 standard elaborates on the relevant aspects of power system design.

The second item is the IEEE 3002 standard, which primarily deals with power system analysis and calculation.

First, the IEEE 3001 standard elaborates on the relevant aspects of power system design.

The second item is the IEEE 3002 standard, which primarily deals with power system analysis and calculation.

The third one is IEEE 3003, which primarily elaborates on matters related to power system grounding.

The fourth part is the IEEE 3004 standard, which primarily elaborates on the relevant content of power system protection and coordination.

The fifth part is the IEEE 3005 standard, which primarily covers hardware power supply design and energy management systems for industrial and commercial power systems.

The fifth part is the IEEE 3005 standard, which primarily covers hardware power supply design and energy management systems for industrial and commercial power systems.

The sixth standard is IEEE 3006, which primarily elaborates on power system reliability analysis. This standard is less commonly applied in distribution systems, low-voltage systems, or medium-voltage systems, and is mainly suitable for reliability assessment of high-voltage power grids.

The seventh one is the IEEE 3007 standard, which primarily elaborates on the maintenance, operation, and safety requirements of various power systems. This standard is essentially an overview document within the IEEE 3000 standard series.

Next, we will introduce another authoritative reference book in the field of low-voltage technology.

Next, we will introduce another authoritative reference book in the field of low-voltage technology.

The full name of BICSI is Building Industry Consulting Services International. It is an industry association that emerged in the United States over the past two to three decades, focusing on the low-voltage sector within the information technology field. Similar to IEEE, BICSI also has a membership system, but its membership tiers are relatively simpler. I once joined as a BICSI member because obtaining their certification required membership first. The annual fee was approximately $100 to $200—I can’t recall the exact amount, as this was ten years ago.

In 2010, I earned one of BICSI’s most significant certifications—RCDD (Registered Communications Distribution Designer). This certification holds high global value, especially in data center projects, where it is often specified as a mandatory qualification. In 2014, the renovation project of Ottawa’s Parliament Hill required RCDD-certified professionals to oversee the IT system upgrades.

In Canada, there are few RCDD holders for two main reasons:  
1. First, the exam is highly challenging. The study materials include a two-volume Design Manual totaling over 2,000 pages, and the exam itself lasts five hours with dozens of pages of questions.  
2. Second, maintaining the certification is cumbersome. Holders must accumulate 45 Continuing Education Credits (CECs) every three years by attending BICSI-hosted seminars or conferences. These events are typically held across the U.S., such as in California or Florida, incurring travel expenses.  

A rough estimate puts the cost of maintaining this certification at around $2,000 over three years, as each credit’s training costs between $50 and $100. At the time, I worked for a large company, which covered these expenses.

At the time, I worked for a large company, which covered these expenses. These large companies covered the relevant expenses, allowing me to sustain myself. At that time, I had held the RCDD certification for approximately six years. Later, due to switching careers to the oil industry, the RCDD certification lost its practical utility, so I no longer participated in the related training and meetings, resulting in the certification’s expiration. After BICSI was established, it published a substantial number of technical guidelines and standards. Now let’s discuss BICSI’s technical guidance series and technical standards. Please check this link, which is BICSI’s official website. You can see that the website has published 4 technical manuals and 13 standards.
The "Telecommunication Cabling Methods Manual" is an essential technical reference. For professionals engaged in communication system design, this is an invaluable reference book.

Next is the “Low-Voltage System Construction Project Guide.” Many of these standards were originally design guidelines but have now been formalized as official standards. For example, the “Best Practices for Electronic Security System Design and Implementation” serves as a crucial technical reference for security system design. Additionally, it covers topics such as antenna design and data center design.

Interested readers can purchase relevant technical reference books based on their needs, either as single volumes or multiple volumes. That concludes today’s sharing.
